headline: Malaysia's former leader serves his sentence at home

sources.title: Malaysia's disgraced former PM leaves jail for house arrest after embezzling millions (BBC)
Malaysia's Najib moved from prison to house arrest after royal clemency (Al Jazeera)
Malaysia's ex-PM Najib Razak arrives home in Kuala Lumpur to serve remainder of jail term under house arrest (CNA)
Malaysian Transport Minister Anthony Loke's resignation to take effect 'immediately' after court grants Najib house arrest (CNA)

chunks.text: On November 10, 2026, Malaysia's former prime minister left prison to serve the rest of his [[sentence]] at home. Malaysia is a country in Southeast Asia. That night, a car with a [[police escort]] {{pulled up}} at his house in the capital. Many reporters {{showed up}}. Officials had [[declared]] the house a [[federal prison]]. Under this [[house arrest]], he must stay home.

verbs.correct: To drive to a place and stop
verbs.why: A taxi pulls up outside the hotel. The school bus pulls up at the corner every morning. That night, a car with a police escort pulled up at his house in Kuala Lumpur.
Fans show up early for every concert. My cousin always shows up late for dinner. Many reporters showed up outside the house that night.

chunks.text: The 73-year-old led Malaysia from 2009 to 2018. He helped {{set up}} a [[state investment fund]], public money the government [[invests]] to help the country grow. Investigators say about 4.5 billion dollars was stolen from the fund. Prosecutors say more than 1 billion dollars {{ended up}} in accounts [[linked to]] him. The [[scandal]] {{brought down}} his government. He denies any [[wrongdoing]].

verbs.wrong: To check how money is spent

verbs.wrong: To be kept secret for years

verbs.why: A big scandal sometimes brings down a powerful leader. Mass protests can bring down a government. The fund scandal brought down his government.

chunks.text: He was {{locked up}} in August 2022, and his 12-year sentence was later cut to six. In September 2026, Malaysia's king gave him a [[conditional pardon]]. Under it, he could spend his last two years at home if he paid a [[fine]] of about 12 million dollars. Supporters {{chipped in}} through a [[fundraiser]], and his party paid on November 6. That day the [[attorney general]], the government's top lawyer, {{held up}} the move. The former leader left prison but was {{sent back}} hours later.

verbs.wrong: To move someone to a hospital
verbs.why: Judges lock up people who commit serious crimes. The police lock up dangerous drivers for the night. He was locked up in August 2022.

verbs.correct: To give money together with others
verbs.wrong: To borrow money from a bank
verbs.why: Coworkers often chip in for a birthday cake. We all chip in for gas on long trips. Supporters chipped in through a fundraiser to pay his fine.

verbs.wrong: To sign a paper for the king
verbs.why: Bad weather often holds up flights. Missing papers hold up the sale of a house. The attorney general held up the move to his home.

verbs.correct: To return someone to a place
verbs.wrong: To move someone to a new city
verbs.why: Border officers send travelers back when they have no visa. The coach sends tired players back to the bench. The former leader left prison but was sent back hours later.

chunks.text: On November 10, a court let the move {{go ahead}}. His lawyer said he deserved it after serving more than half his time. [[Critics]] {{spoke out}} against the decision. They say Malaysian law has no rule for house arrest, and that it hurts the fight against [[corruption]]. The transport minister {{stepped down}} [[in protest]]. He said in September he would quit, but {{stayed on}} when the prime minister asked. The former leader is [[appealing]] a second sentence of 15 years, {{handed down}} in December 2025, which starts after his house arrest.

verbs.why: The game goes ahead even in light rain. Our trip goes ahead if the roads are clear. On November 10, a court let the move go ahead.

verbs.why: Students often speak out against unfair rules. Many doctors speak out about the dangers of smoking. Critics spoke out against the decision to let him go home.

verbs.wrong: To give a speech to voters
verbs.why: Some coaches step down after a bad season. A leader often steps down after a big scandal. The transport minister stepped down in protest.

mainIdea.s: Malaysia's former leader moved from prison to his own house after the king reduced his punishment. Critics say the decision hurts efforts against corruption, and one minister quit over it.
mainIdea.why: The king gave him a conditional pardon, and he now serves his sentence under house arrest. Critics spoke out, and the transport minister stepped down.

mainIdea.s: Malaysia's government chose to let its jailed ex-prime minister spend his remaining years at home. Most ministers backed this plan, saying the house arrest would save money and calm voters.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the king gave the pardon, not the government. The attorney general held up the move, and the transport minister stepped down in protest.

mainIdea.s: A former prime minister of Malaysia began a new trial about money missing from a public fund. Prosecutors expect the case to take two years, and he must wait in prison while it continues.
mainIdea.why: This story is about him leaving prison for house arrest. Supporters chipped in to pay his fine, and a court let the move go ahead.

tf.s: Malaysia's former prime minister will serve the rest of his sentence at home.
tf.why: A car with a police escort pulled up at his house in Kuala Lumpur, which officials declared a federal prison.

tf.s: The former prime minister admits that he took money from the fund.
tf.why: He denies any wrongdoing, although prosecutors say more than 1 billion dollars ended up in accounts linked to him.

tf.s: The fund scandal brought down his government.
tf.why: The scandal over the state investment fund cost him and his government their power.

tf.s: His party refused to pay the fine for his house arrest.
tf.why: Supporters chipped in through a fundraiser, and his party paid the fine on November 6.

tf.s: The attorney general held up his move from prison to his home.
tf.why: The attorney general wanted legal answers first, so the former leader was sent back to prison for a few days.

tf.s: Malaysia's transport minister praised the decision to let him go home.
tf.why: The transport minister stepped down in protest after the court let the move go ahead.

lines.text: Did you see the news from Malaysia? The former prime minister is serving the rest of his prison sentence at home.
At home? How does that work?
Officials declared his house a federal prison. A car with a police escort {{pulled up}} late at night, and lots of reporters {{showed up}}.
I bet it's [[the talk of the town]] in Kuala Lumpur.
It is. He was {{locked up}} in 2022 over a huge scandal at a state fund he helped {{set up}}.
How much money are we talking about?
Investigators say about 4.5 billion dollars. Prosecutors say more than a billion {{ended up}} in accounts linked to him.
No, he denies any wrongdoing. But the scandal {{brought down}} his government.
So why is he going home now?
The king gave him a conditional pardon. His supporters {{chipped in}} to pay a fine of about 12 million dollars.
That kind of thing really [[rubs people the wrong way]]. It looks like powerful people are [[above the law]].
That's what critics say. His lawyer says he has served more than half his time. But many have {{spoken out}} against it, and the transport minister {{stepped down}}.
He said he would leave if this happened, and he [[kept his word]].
No. The attorney general {{held it up}}, and he was {{sent back}} to prison for a few days. Then a court let it {{go ahead}}.
And it sounds [[far from over]], since he still faces a second sentence.
